name: The Cassandra Afterimage

detectability.signature: Ghost-light overlays: spectra showing two epochs superimposed, offset by millennia

proximity: Weak ghost images overlay the live starfield
Comms pick up whispers of broadcasts centuries ended
contact: Crew glimpse coherent scenes from the deep past playing against the hull
Clocks disagree by fractions of a second, harmlessly
prolonged_exposure: Mild temporal disorientation and vivid historical dreams
Occasional memory bleed confusing lived events with echoed ones

phenomena: Visible echoes of events that happened millions of years ago
Radio traffic arriving faintly before it is broadcast
Ships appearing briefly older or newer while crossing echo pockets
hazards: Memory confusion between present events and temporal echoes
opportunities: Archaeological significance: direct recordings of extinct civilizations
Data valuable to scientific institutions across half the sector
known_incidents: Historians confirmed the fate of the drowned world Vess by watching its last storm replay across the Afterimage for eleven nights
A treasure hunter spent her fortune chasing an echoed fleet that had already been salvaged ten thousand years before her arrival
description: Space here plays old light. Faint and slightly translucent, scenes from twelve million years ago drift through the volume: unfamiliar constellations, the death throes of an unnamed star, storms on a world whose oceans are long gone. The overlays waver like reflections on moving water, visible to the naked eye and maddening to cameras.

The echo pockets drift slowly, never quite repeating, their strength waxing without discernible schedule. Crossing one, crews catch fragments of ancient radio and glimpses of events that concluded eons before their species learned fire. Nothing here can touch a ship; the past, mercifully, is only watching.

The Afterimage settled a dozen academic wars in a decade, offering direct footage of eras known only from sediment and guesswork. Historians queued research vessels for years to watch the drowning of Vess unfold night after night. The phenomenon resists every theory of residual light, and the leading explanation is politely described as unsettling.

Archives license the observations widely, and pilgrimage tourism is technically banned and practically constant. Treasure hunters remain a nuisance, chasing echoed fleets that died rich and rotted poorer than their ghosts suggest. The past here is harmless, which somehow makes it harder to stop watching.
